transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Erin Moss (NovusHealth CTO), Arjun Rao (Lead ML), Lisa Kim (DevOps)
Shared artifacts: deck: https://redwood.example/decks/hosted-chatflow.pdf (short link), benchmark sheet: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/novus-quick-bench.csv

Summary (auto-gen, may be partial):
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics — streaming behavior, key generation parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), and recommended retry/backoff patterns for unstable networks. Customer concerned about p99 latency, cost per 1k tokens, and safe fallbacks for critical patient-data flows. Next step: trial keys, benchmark, 30m POC kickoff.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Alex from Redwood, I'm the account lead. Samira will walk through the runtime and demo the hosted API streaming behavior. How's Novus doing today?
[00:08] Erin: Doing well, thanks. We got a quick agenda, right? want to see the chat patterns and what happens when connections drop, and we want to understand parameter knobs so we can set SLAs.
[00:15] Samira: Yep that's the plan. We'll show a live chat gen -> streaming -> and then simulate a network blip to demonstrate resume/retry patterns. I'll also call out cost tradeoffs and quick rules of thumb for temperature/top_p and token limits. 
[00:28] Lisa: Great. We're particularly sensitive about p99 latency for clinical triage flows; anything that blocks doctors is a problem.
[00:35] Alex: Totally. We'll focus on both latency-first patterns and cost-aware batching approaches.
[00:40] Samira: Ok jumping in: Redwood's hosted API supports chunked streaming over SSE and WebSocket; our SDK defaults to SSE in the JS client. The main knobs you care about for generation are: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, presence/ frequency penalties, stop sequences, and also stream_chunk_size which controls how often partial tokens flush — lower chunk size reduces perceived latency but can increase overhead.
[01:05] Arjun: Can you show how that looks in practice? like code and then the streaming trace?
[01:09] Samira: Sure — demo time. (typing) I'm calling /v1/generate with model: rw-large-v1, mode: chat, stream: true, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 256, stop: ["\n\n"]. I'll open the trace view in the Console so you can see token-level latency.
[01:30] Samira: (shares screen) here's the console trace — you can see initial response latency is ~120ms for small prompts, tokens arrive in ~40ms increments. When I lower stream_chunk_size from 64 to 16, the first token appears a bit faster, but we started to make more smaller network writes. That's a CPU/egress trade off.
[01:55] Erin: Are those numbers from your hosted cluster or representative of our geography? we are region EU-west.
[02:02] Samira: Good question — these are in us-central; we have EU regions and latency is typically +30–60ms depending on peering. We can pin region in the API call or via account settings to keep it in eu-west-2.
[02:18] Lisa: If the stream connection drops mid-response, do you buffer server-side or is it client responsibility to retry?
[02:24] Samira: By default, we don't hold open unlimited server-side state for streaming connections — we maintain the model KV cache for the request for a short window. For recommender flows where you need durable resume, we recommend clients record the last event_id or token index and re-issue a non-streamed generate with prefix=existing chat history and include the partial response as context. We also have a resumable token API in Private/Dedicated that can checkpoint large KV caches — but for hosted, the lightweight pattern is idempotency + prefix replay.
[02:55] Arjun: So the pattern is: detect disconnect, then re-call generate with same prompt and role history, plus set max_tokens to remaining tokens?
[03:03] Samira: Exactly. If you want to avoid double-writing to your UI, use an idempotency key and a client-side merging strategy. For aggressive low-latency usecases, we show a 'resume' example in the playbook I'll send.
[03:16] Alex: Quick interjection on retries: our recommended backoff is jittered exponential with caps — start at 200ms, then 500ms, 1s, up to 8s. For 5xx or transient network errors we retry; for 4xx like 429 we surface rate-limit headers and respect Retry-After. We also recommend circuit-breakers for persistent failures.
[03:38] Lisa: For 429s, is there a token-cost impact if we re-submit? how do we avoid double billing for partial responses?
[03:46] Samira: Billing is per token generated — if your client resubmits identical request and the model re-generates same tokens, that will count again. For that reason, use idempotency-key semantics and server-side dedupe when possible. We also provide streaming offsets in the response so your client can checkpoint progress and avoid re-requesting already-received content.
[04:05] Erin: Can you demo a simulated drop?
[04:08] Samira: Yep — I'll use the network tab to throttle and drop. (pause) Ok triggering now.
[04:18] [04:19] Samira: Connection dropped — console shows aborted stream. In the client logs you can see last_event_id: 97 and last_token_index: 34. I'll re-issue a generate with prefix up to token index 34 and set max_tokens to 222, with same idempotency key.
[04:37] [04:45] Samira: Re-issued — response resumed, and the client merges seamlessly. You can see the UI-level glitch was minimal, and overall p50 didn't change much.
[04:55] Arjun: That resume flow seems workable. how about when we want deterministic outputs for critical templated responses?
[05:02] Samira: For determinism keep temperature near 0.0, set top_p low (e.g., 0.1–0.3), pin a specific model version, and use stop sequences to tightly bound responses. Also use a smaller context window to reduce subtle nondeterminism from extra tokens. But note you trade off diversity, so for free-text triage summaries you might want a slightly higher temperature and then run an evaluation set through Redwood Optimize to monitor regressions.
[05:29] Lisa: Can you touch on concurrency? we will have multiple clinics hitting the same endpoint concurrently; will queued requests cause higher latency?
[05:36] Samira: Redwood's serving runtime supports request-level concurrency with smart batching. For latency-first SLOs we recommend a low batch window (2–5ms) and per-route concurrency limits to pin p99. Dedicated customers can reserve capacity to eliminate noisy neighbor effects. For hosted, you can configure per-account concurrency and we'll surface throttling in the Console.
[05:58] Alex: Also mention auto-burst: hosted accounts can be set with burst to handle occasional bursts but that's bounded; for predictable throughput dedicated is better.
[06:06] Erin: We're likely to start with hosted for evaluation. We need to understand cost per 1k tokens at our expected scale — say 10M tokens/month.
[06:14] Alex: We'll send a cost estimate; rough ballpark: model rw-large-v1 ~ $X per 1k tokens (we'll fill exact numbers in the follow-up), and you can reduce costs with quantized variants or by using cached prefixes and completion-only paths. Also Redwood Optimize suggests batching and cache TTLs by observing traffic patterns.
[06:33] Arjun: How does cache keying work? we have patient-specific context that must never leak.
[06:39] Samira: Cache keys are namespaced per account and you can mark sensitive keys as non-cacheable. For PII flows we recommend disabling shared prefix caching and enable per-request encryption via KMS. We do not share KV cache across accounts.
[06:57] Lisa: What about compliance — SOC 2, data residency?
[07:01] Alex: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II certified, we support SAML/SSO, audit logs, and EU data residency options for hosted. For stronger requirements we recommend Private deployment that gives you VPC/RBAC + HSM/KMS. We'll attach the security pack after this call.
[07:18] Erin: Good — send the SOC and pen-test summaries.
[07:21] Alex: Will do.
[07:23] Samira: Back to retries: in practice we recommend separating idempotent operations (like embeddings) from non-idempotent chat generation. For chat, use idempotency keys per user turn. If you need at-least-once semantics, handle duplicate text client-side. We also show a pattern for optimistic UI: show partial streaming tokens as they arrive and mark responses as provisional until the final commit event.
[07:49] Arjun: Any example of exponential backoff config?
[07:53] Samira: Our playbook: initial=200ms, multiplier=2, max=8000ms, jitter=full. For 429s respect Retry-After, and on repeated 5xx escalate to an on-call alert after N retries.
[08:07] Lisa: Curious about long-running KV caches — if we timeout a stream and re-issue, is the previous KV cache still valid?
[08:13] Samira: We keep ephemeral KV cache around for a short TTL (configurable per-account) — default is 30s in hosted; Dedicated/Private can increase this. If you need longer-lived context, persist the chat history yourself and replay on resume.
[08:27] Alex: We sometimes recommend summarization-in-the-loop: periodically compress prior turns into a summary token so your replay payload stays small. That reduces token costs on replays.
[08:36] Erin: Let's talk parameters — what's the practical effect of temperature 0.2 vs 0.8 for our triage text?
[08:42] Samira: 0.2 gives more deterministic, focused outputs suitable for templated clinical messages. 0.8 increases creativity and variance; useful for patient-facing educational text where variety is desired. We recommend running your eval set through Optimize to tune temperature per intent.
[08:56] Arjun: How do stop sequences interplay with streaming?
[09:00] Samira: Stop sequences tell the model where to stop generating; streaming will keep sending tokens until it hits a stop or max_tokens. If you set a strong stop like '\n\nEND\n', you'll get deterministic truncation, which is nice for prompt templates.
[09:13] Lisa: Are there examples for partial response reconciliation? we want to avoid showing duplicates when a resume happens.
[09:18] Samira: Yes — the client should track last_token_index and the server's event id; on resume, request only the remaining tokens and append. If you can't guarantee server-side dedupe, use idempotent keys and server-side merge logic. The guide has a snippet for JS and Python.
[09:36] Arjun: Ok can we dig into rate limits? How do we know when to switch to fallback model?
[09:42] Samira: We expose per-route usage metrics in the Console. For fallbacks we recommend a rule-based policy: if p95 latency > X or error rate > Y, route to a smaller model (e.g., rw-medium) or cached completions. The Console can automate this with simple routing policies that check health metrics.
[09:59] Erin: Demo the Console policy?
[10:02] Samira: (navigates) here's a policy: primary model rw-large-v1, fallback rw-medium-v1, failover window 30s, min confidence threshold 0.6. When traffic spikes, you can see automatic routing in the trace.
[10:20] Alex: Also mention that fallbacks reduce cost and keep availability; Optimize can suggest which smaller model maintains acceptable quality for a given prompt set.
[10:29] Erin: How do we validate quality across fallbacks?
[10:32] Samira: Redwood Optimize runs prompt-based evals and does regression alerts. We'll run your clinical prompt set and give a delta score across models. You can set an automatic rollback if quality drops beyond a threshold.
[10:45] Lisa: Ok that's helpful. Another ops question: we're behind a corporate proxy that rewrites TLS headers — will that break streaming?
[10:53] Samira: Sometimes proxies buffer chunked responses which can make streaming appear delayed; in that case we recommend websocket transport or adjust chunking so the proxy flushes more frequently. We'll share a troubleshooting note for common proxy issues.
[11:10] Arjun: Anything about concurrency limits per API key?
[11:14] Alex: Yes — per-key concurrency is enforced; default is 20 concurrent requests for hosted, configurable up to account-level caps. If you need higher concurrency, we can propose dedicated capacity.
[11:24] Erin: We're planning a pilot with 3 clinics and about 200 reqs/min peak, mostly small prompts. Does that map well to hosted?
[11:31] Samira: That should be fine for hosted. We'll size the expected token volume and give a recommended concurrency plus burst profile in the follow-up.
[11:40] Arjun: Any tips on prompt engineering for shorter token counts?
[11:44] Samira: Use instruction templates, avoid verbose system messages, and leverage placeholders. Also use stop sequences to prevent run-on; and use compression/summarization for older turns. Optimize has an auto-suggest for prompt length reduction.
[12:00] Lisa: Can you show a sample SDK call in Python for streaming?
[12:04] Samira: Sure — (typing) from redwood import Client; c = Client(api_key=...); gen = c.generate(model='rw-large-v1', stream=True, temperature=0.2, max_tokens=256, prompt=...).for_each_chunk(lambda chunk: print(chunk.text)) — this yields chunked text events and metadata with token_index and event_id.
[12:26] Arjun: And how to surface partial scores or token-level logits for moderation?
[12:31] Samira: We don't expose raw logits in hosted, but we provide per-token probabilities in Dedicated/Private for advanced uses. For hosted moderation we provide async moderation endpoints and content filters integrated in the pipeline.
[12:45] Erin: What about embedding alignment — we plan to use embeddings + chat for retrieval. Is there a recommended pattern?
[12:50] Samira: Typical is: generate embedding for query, retrieve top-k docs, build a condensed prompt with retrieved docs + system instructions, then call generate. Cache embeddings for repeated queries and shard embedding requests for throughput. We'll share a retrieval-augmented generation example.
[13:10] Lisa: Can you highlight the admin controls in Console we should know about?
[13:14] Samira: In Console: per-route rate limits, API keys, SSO users and roles, audit logs, and per-model rollout policies. You can also view cost by token type and per-route token breakdown.
[13:28] Arjun: Any gotchas for JS clients around streaming in mobile browsers?
[13:33] Samira: Mobile browsers sometimes throttle background tabs and can coalesce writes. Use web-socket transport for critical mobile use cases or heartbeat to keep the tab alive.
[13:44] Erin: Let's talk about the sample benchmark you mentioned — what will you run?
[13:48] Samira: We'll run a 24–72 hour small bench: run your eval prompts at scaled rates to measure p50/p95/p99 latency, token usage, and error rate across regions. We'll include a column for cost estimates and a recommended route config.
[14:04] Alex: We'll need Arjun's sample dataset to kick this off.
[14:07] Arjun: I'll share a de-identified batch by Monday.
[14:10] Lisa: Security again — are logs redacted?
[14:13] Alex: We support log redaction and configurable retention; you can disable full-text logging for sensitive flows. Also SSO provisioning and role limits to restrict who can view traces.
[14:24] Samira: One more advanced note on retries: for streaming we emit a final 'completion' event; if that's missing, treat it as incomplete. For very long outputs, you might want to checkpoint summaries every N tokens to reduce the cost of replays.
[14:40] Arjun: Does your SDK surface the retry-after and the cloud provider error codes?
[14:44] Samira: Yes — we forward upstream headers including Retry-After and a normalized error code field in the JSON error payload so you can programmatically decide.
[14:54] Erin: Ok we're almost at time. Quick recap of asks?
[14:58] Alex: Action items: Alex send quickstart and pricing, Samira send playbook + benchmark template, Arjun share de-identified dataset, schedule POC kickoff for next week.
[15:10] Erin: Sounds good. Appreciate the demo.
[15:13] Alex: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with the artifacts and a calendar invite.
[15:17] (call ends)

Notes on transcription quality: speaker overlap and some proper nouns may be slightly off (e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as 'K-V cash'). Intent and key numbers recorded accurately in Console artifacts.

End of transcript.
